hook: Norbert Wiener was a mathematical prodigy who earned a bachelor's degree from Tufts College at 14 and a PhD in philosophy from Harvard at 19, then studied with Bertrand Russell in Cambridge and David Hilbert in Gottingen. He joined MIT's Department of Mathematics in 1919 and remained there for 45 years, doing foundational work in stochastic processes, harmonic analysis, and what became known as the Wiener process. During the Second World War he worked on statistical prediction methods for anti-aircraft fire control, research that pushed him toward a broader theory of control and communication. In 1948 he published Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine, founding the field of cybernetics and giving later computing and AI research a vocabulary for feedback loops. His 1950 book The Human Use of Human Beings extended these ideas to society, warning early about the social effects of automation. He became an MIT Institute Professor in 1959 and died in 1964 while traveling in Stockholm, Sweden.

quick_facts: Founded the field of cybernetics with his 1948 book Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine.
A mathematical prodigy, he earned a bachelor's degree from Tufts College at 14 and a PhD in philosophy from Harvard at 19.
Spent 45 years on MIT's mathematics faculty, becoming an MIT Institute Professor in 1959.
His World War II era work on anti-aircraft fire control prediction contributed to the foundations of statistical filtering and control theory.
Warned publicly about automation's social effects in his 1950 book The Human Use of Human Beings.
Received the Bocher Memorial Prize (1933) and the National Medal of Science (1964).

achievements.title: Founded cybernetics
achievements.impact: His 1948 book Cybernetics established a unified framework for control, communication, and feedback across mechanical, biological, and social systems, later drawn on by computing and AI research.

achievements.title: Wartime prediction theory and fire control
achievements.impact: Developed statistical filtering methods for anti-aircraft targeting during World War II, foundational to later control theory and signal processing.

achievements.title: Wiener process and stochastic mathematics
achievements.impact: His mathematical treatment of Brownian motion became a standard tool across engineering, physics, and finance.

achievements.title: The Human Use of Human Beings (1950)
achievements.impact: Brought cybernetic ideas to a general audience and raised early public questions about automation's effect on labor and society.

achievements.title: MIT Institute Professor
achievements.impact: Held MIT's highest faculty distinction, capping a 45-year career on the mathematics faculty.
